cards.q: What is route summarization and why does it matter?
cards.a: It combines multiple more-specific routes into a single less-specific route, e.g. 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.3.0/24 become 10.1.0.0/22; it reduces routing-table size, limits routing updates, improves scalability, and contains route instability. Core idea: advertise one larger prefix instead of many smaller prefixes.

cards.q: How do you calculate a summary prefix from the network addresses?
cards.a: Find the common leftmost bits of the network addresses, count them as the prefix length, set the remaining bits to 0, and verify coverage; e.g. 10.1.0.0/24, .1, .2, and .3 share 10.1 plus six bits of the third octet (000000), giving /22 and summary 10.1.0.0/22.

cards.q: What are the steps to compute a route summary?
cards.a: List all network addresses; convert the changing octet(s) to binary; find the common leftmost bits; count those bits as the summary prefix length; set all remaining bits to 0; and verify the summary covers the intended networks.

cards.q: Why must a summary be aligned, and what are valid /22 boundaries?
cards.a: A /22 has 10 host bits and groups 4 × /24 networks, so valid third-octet boundaries are 0, 4, 8, 12, ... 252; 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.4.0/22 are valid, but 10.1.1.0/22 is invalid because the boundary does not align with the block size.

cards.q: What addresses does a summary prefix actually cover?
cards.a: Every address inside the prefix, not just the currently existing subnets; for example 10.1.0.0/22 covers 10.1.0.0–10.1.3.255, so summarizing 10.1.0.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24, and 10.1.3.0/24 also covers the nonexistent 10.1.2.0/24, which can cause black-hole routing.

cards.q: What is the difference among route summarization, supernetting, and CIDR?
cards.a: Route summarization combines multiple routes into one less-specific route; supernetting combines contiguous address blocks into a larger prefix; CIDR is classless addressing using arbitrary prefix lengths. The same aggregation, such as four /24s becoming 192.168.0.0/22, can be called a supernet and a route summary depending on context.

cards.q: Where is route summarization typically used in a network hierarchy?
cards.a: At aggregation boundaries such as distribution to core, where a distribution router advertises a single 10.1.0.0/22 toward the core instead of four /24 routes; it is a common hierarchical-network design practice.

cards.q: How do you perform route summarization in OSPF?
cards.a: An ABR performs inter-area summarization with area range, e.g. router ospf 1, area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0; external routes are summarized on an ASBR using the summary-address command.

cards.q: How do you perform manual route summarization in EIGRP?
cards.a: Configure it on the outgoing interface with ip summary-address eigrp 100 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0 (under router eigrp 100 with network statements); the interface then advertises the summary instead of the more-specific routes.

cards.q: How do you aggregate routes in BGP?
cards.a: Use router bgp 65001, aggregate-address 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0; adding summary-only suppresses the more-specific component routes from being advertised along with the aggregate.

cards.q: What are the benefits of route summarization?
cards.a: Smaller routing tables, fewer routing updates, better scalability by hiding internal details, faster convergence (subnet changes need not affect every router), and flap containment where instability in a more-specific route stays within a smaller part of the network.

cards.q: What are the risks of route summarization?
cards.a: Black-hole routing when traffic for an unused portion of the summary reaches the summarizing router and is discarded, overly broad summaries that include another network or routing domain, and loss of routing detail that makes troubleshooting or path selection less precise.

cards.q: Does a summary automatically override more-specific routes?
cards.a: No; routers use longest-prefix match. With 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.2.0/24 both present, traffic for 10.1.2.10 follows the more specific /24 — the specific route wins over the summary.

cards.q: Do three /24 networks automatically form an exact /22?
cards.a: No; a /22 contains four /24 networks, so three networks alone do not make an exact /22 — the resulting summary would also cover the missing fourth /24.

cards.q: Which OSPF command summarizes inter-area routes versus external routes?
cards.a: area X range is used for inter-area route summarization by an ABR; external-route summarization uses summary-address on an ASBR.

cards.q: Where is EIGRP manual summarization configured?
cards.a: On the outgoing interface with the ip summary-address eigrp command, not globally under the routing process.

Purpose: represent multiple routes with one less-specific route; method: common leftmost bits; prefix = number of common bits; the boundary must be aligned; OSPF uses area range (inter-area, ABR) and summary-address (external, ASBR); EIGRP uses ip summary-address eigrp; BGP uses aggregate-address; main benefit smaller routing tables and less churn; main risks overly broad summaries and black holes; longest-prefix match wins.

cards.q: What is the one-minute exam memory for summarization?
cards.a: Many specific routes → find common leftmost bits → create an aligned less-specific prefix → advertise one summary → smaller routing table → less routing churn; remember: common bits give the summary prefix, a correct boundary makes it valid, the summary covers the entire prefix, more-specific routes win, and a too-broad summary can create a black hole.
